articles.title: Tesla’s new Dog and Sentry modes take care even when you don’t
articles.summary: Tesla’s new software update includes a Dog Mode, which will keep your pup at a comfortable temperature while you’re out of the car, and a Sentry Mode, which you can enable to have the car essentially guard itself, using its exterior cameras to monitor movement nearby and identify potential threats.
articles.body: Tesla has just announced a pair of new modes that make great use of the abundance of sensors and technology inside the company’s cars to make a driver’s life a little easier. First and most endearing is the Dog Mode: this will keep your pup at a comfortable temperature while you’re out of the car, and it’ll use the jumbo display at the center to show a message for passersby that you’ll be returning soon. The other major addition is Sentry Mode, which you can enable to have the car essentially guard itself, using its exterior cameras to monitor movement nearby and identify potential threats. [Media: To turn on Dog Mode, you just go into your climate control settings and select the very literal “DOG” option, where you’ll be able to adjust the temperature to a preference within preset limits. Owners of non-canine pets would presumably be equally well-served by the functionality, should they find themselves driving with a furry friend. Tesla rightly advises that you still check local laws about leaving pets unattended in the car before relying on this new feature. The Sentry Mode is really just a logical upgrade of a basic car alarm. If the Tesla detects a person leaning on it, for example, it’ll count that as a minimal threat, switch into an Alert state, and present a notification on its dash display that it’s taking a video recording of what’s happening. Should a window be smashed, however, the Alarm state is triggered, the display increases brightness, and the speakers start blaring out music at max volume. All of that is on top of the obvious and standard response of the car alarm going off. Sentry Mode needs to be enabled every time a user wants to rely on it, and it’ll download a video recording of any incidents to a formatted USB drive, should you have one around to plug in before turning the mode on. The new update is rolling out to Model 3 cars in the United States from today, to be followed by Model S and Model X vehicles built after August 2017. It also includes improvements to dashcam functionality, though it’s still missing the promised Camper & Party mode that was supposed to arrive last year.

articles.title: Arturia adds proper sound design tools to its AstroLab synths
articles.summary: You can finally create fully customized sounds on Arturia’s AstroLab line of stage keyboards with the 2.0 firmware update.
articles.body: Arturia’s AstroLab series was already amongst the best stage keyboards out there. They essentially put the company’s AnalogLab suite of vintage synth emulations, sampled pianos, and original instrument plugins into playable hardware. But they were ultimately glorified preset browsers. You could lightly tweak patches using the four macro controls, or dial in some effects, but you couldn’t do any real sound design. That’s all changed now with the AstroLab 2.0 update. The latest firmware adds a Sound Edit menu that lets you dig into the individual parameters of any instrument. It’s not super intuitive to quickly fire up a blank patch from the instrument of your choosing, and these more advanced sound design tools require some menu diving, but once you get there, creating custom sounds is pretty easy. The quickest way to build patches from scratch is to make a custom category for templates and save initialized patches for each instrument there. For example, upload a basic Moog bass patch template from the AnalogLab desktop app, then you can tweak it to your heart’s content and save it as a completely new sound directly on the hardware. Since a firmware update can’t add more knobs and buttons, you still have to make all the changes with the four macro knobs and page through settings four at a time. It can be a bit time-consuming, and you’re not going to do a bunch of on-the-fly tweaking, but it gets the job done. Arturia has also added a new collection of multisampled instruments, including pianos, strings, and brass sections that offer more realistic acoustic instruments. This is one area where its competition clearly outclassed the AstroLab, but this should help close the gap. In total, there are 67 new patches. Lastly, Arturia has also made a number of small quality-of-life improvements. The octave LEDs will now show transposition, aftertouch has been tweaked to feel more responsive, and app connectivity has supposedly been made more reliable. While connectivity with the desktop AnalogLab seems rock-solid, the mobile AstroLab Connect app seems as flaky as ever. AstroLab 2.0 is available now as a free update for all AstroLab keyboards.

articles.body: British comedian and TV star Jim Davidson has broken his silence on his new romance with Maria Rice-Mundy, just weeks after announcing that his planned sixth wedding to former partner Natasha had been called off.Speaking to the Daily Mail, the 72-year-old Big Break star claimed that he and Natasha, 49, actually ended their relationship for the final time around three months ago. According to Davidson, Natasha was the one who called time on their three-year relationship, which he described as turbulent and marked by repeated break-ups.Davidson is now dating Maria, 60, a former beauty pageant winner and television presenter who co-hosted Sale of the Century and Bob's Your Uncle with the late Bob Monkhouse in the late 1980s.Jim Davidson calls Maria 'too good to be true'Davidson revealed that Maria is not a recent acquaintance. The comedian said the pair have known each other for decades and have recently gone on several dinner dates while exploring their relationship.“Maria's not a new lady. I've known her for years. In fact, I gatecrashed her wedding 30 years ago. She is too good to be true,” Davidson told the publication.Although he acknowledged that he is still coming to terms with his split from Natasha, Davidson said Maria has made a strong impression on him.“I'll be honest, I am not short of ladies who want to date me but Maria has something special about her. She makes me feel like I'm not as useless as I've been made out to be,” he said.Davidson also insisted that he is not rushing into another marriage, explaining that he and Maria are currently seeing where their relationship goes.“Maria and I have had some dinners together and we are seeing how it goes,” he said.'I would just like to not be lonely'The comedian was candid about his emotional state following the end of his relationship with Natasha, admitting that he has not completely moved on.“It takes a while to get over something like this,” Davidson said, adding that he “would just like to not be lonely.”He claimed that the relationship had been difficult for some time, saying the couple would repeatedly split and reconcile.“Natasha dumped me three months ago. She said I had given her no choice — but to be honest it was up and down and we would split up every month,” he said.Despite their separation, Davidson maintained that there is no animosity between them and said he would still support Natasha if she needed him.“If my ex Tash is ever in the s**t, she can call me and I'll be there for her,” he said.New romance comes weeks after sixth wedding was cancelledDavidson announced in early September that his planned wedding to Natasha would no longer take place. The couple had been due to marry at Hampton Court, a venue that carried a deliberate reference to King Henry VIII and his six wives.The comedian had previously spoken enthusiastically about marrying Natasha for a sixth time, but later described their separation as a “grown up separation” and said there was “no bad blood” between them.He attributed their break-up partly to their conflicting schedules, saying they had struggled to make enough time for each other.The cancellation also reportedly left Davidson having to absorb a £10,000 deposit on the planned wedding.Davidson and Maria have been dating for weeksThe new relationship emerged publicly after a source told the Daily Mail that Davidson and Maria had been dating for several weeks.According to the source, Davidson has already become strongly attracted to Maria and had shared a picture of her on Facebook. The pair have reportedly enjoyed several dinner dates, with the source describing Maria as “very giggly around him.”Maria, who is a mother of three, is also competing as a finalist in the Ms Great Britain Classic 2026 national final.His relationship history and fifth divorceDavidson's romance with Natasha began in early 2024, following the breakdown of his 14-year marriage to Michelle Cotton.At Nigel Farage's 60th birthday celebration at Boisdale's in Canary Wharf, Davidson arrived with Natasha and openly spoke about his plans to marry her. At the time, he described himself as “completely smitten” and suggested he had finally found “the one.”He even renamed his £350,000 yacht Lady Natasha, after it had previously been named Princess Mitchie after his former wife.Davidson had earlier announced his divorce from Michelle in 2023 after around two decades together. The pair had married in 2009, and Davidson said at the time that he remained on good terms with her.Speaking about the end of that marriage, he said, “There you go, the divorce came through today, so it's done. I'm divorced again, my fifth divorce.”He also said he planned to remain in contact with Michelle but found it too painful to see the dogs they had shared.Davidson has been married five timesDavidson's first marriage was to his childhood sweetheart Sue Walpole in 1971. They had a daughter, Sarah Walpole-Davidson, before divorcing a year later.He married Julie Gullick in 1981, and they had a son, Cameron. The couple divorced in 1986.In 1987, Davidson married journalist and television presenter Alison Holloway, but the marriage lasted less than two years.His fourth marriage came in 1990, when he married former Page 3 model Tracy Hilton. Their marriage lasted around a decade, and they had three children together - Charlie, Fred and Elsie.His fifth marriage was to Michelle Cotton in 2009. articles.title: Our first five impressions of Googlebooks — exciting but underbaked
articles.summary: Googlebook first hands-on impressions: Google’s new laptop OS shows lots of promise if you own an Android phone and want a laptop to match. But there’s lots to improve.
articles.body: Googlebooks are here. The first models went on sale Sunday, October 4th, and we received review units of all five Googlebooks about 24 hours ago. Since then, we’ve been in a mad dash to put the devices through their paces and get a check on what it’s like to use these Android laptops. At first glance, Googlebooks feel very Chromebook-ish, and at times a little janky. But Google has some great new ideas afoot on how a laptop and phone interact. You can already link your phone to a Windows laptop to sync your notifications and mirror your whole iPhone on macOS. But Googlebooks allow you to take actions on your phone from your laptop in a way that feels natural. When it works, of course. Here are all the things we’re learning, feeling, and thinking about so far with Googlebooks. The good, the bad, and the weird. The Android phone integrations are slick [Image: All your Android phone apps are here in their own app drawer. And your phone files are readily available in the Googlebook Files app. Googlebooks revolve around using an Android phone, and Google’s execution here is great. Setting up a Googlebook with an Android phone is simple and painless. The out-of-box experience is pretty intuitive, prompting you to pair your phone by scanning a QR code, sign into your Google account, and then download some of the apps you’ve already installed on your phone. It’s similar to the most recent Chromebooks, but it’s intuitive. Casting apps from your phone, migrating a task from your phone to your laptop with a single click, accessing your phone files on your laptop, and getting your phone notifications on your laptop all work well. These are smart ideas that let you keep your focus on your laptop while you work, but some of them are rough around the edges — in some cases, literally. App casting allows you to use your phone apps directly on a Googlebook, and it feels natural to launch them straight from an app drawer on a laptop instead of mirroring your whole phone screen. But it also means your two separate app drawers on a Googlebook will have duplicate apps. And there’s nothing to stop you from running a desktop version and mobile version at the same time — even with Chrome. That should be easily ignorable, but clicking on synced notifications (like Slack) can open a casted app instead of a web app or native app on the Googlebook. And casted apps sometimes have pixelated text or oddly proportioned UI. They also look and feel just a touch sluggish in animations and scrolling compared to the native desktop apps. [Image: [Image: Google’s Continue On feature, which temporarily pins an app you’re using on your phone to the Googlebook taskbar, is super neat. If I open a spreadsheet on my phone, I can easily transfer it over to the laptop with one click. Brilliant! Except, most apps I tried don’t sync over to the Googlebook with that functionality — not even Google Maps or Calendar. It seems mostly for Google Docs and Sheets for now, and it’s awesome for those. Lastly, pulling files directly off your phone from your laptop just works. It’s great! The Glowbar is fun but not incredibly useful [Image: A wee bit of fanfare when you close the lid. I love a fancy light show. Google’s Glowbars on these laptops offer Googlebooks a signature flair, but they don’t do much. It’s on the lid, facing away from you, and it’s normally illuminated white while you use the laptop. It alternates colors when you talk to Gemini, and closing the lid temporarily displays a Google-y rainbow before it sleeps. The most useful function is that it shows the laptop charge level. But I was hoping for some cool animated lights to show a trickling charge while you have the lid closed or something. It just pulses a few times with green, yellow, or red light to give an approximate charge level when you plug in or unplug a power cable. And the Glowbar that actually faces you on Lenovo’s optional AI Mouse is just a glorified RGB strip that you pick the colors for — it doesn’t sync up to the lid lights. These little light strips are just begging to be tinkered with. I hope Google does much more here. At least start by showing a constant charge level that slowly fills up the strip. Android apps are still a mixed bag, even with Google’s new desktop ratings [Image: Some of these ratings feel a little more lax in practice than I had initially hoped. I love that Google is now flagging Play Store apps with desktop ratings. Browsing apps on a Googlebook classifies them in five categories: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, Compatible with desktop, Better on the website, and Built for mobile. We haven’t found many “Made for desktop” apps outside of core Google ones and a few other examples like CapCut Pad and BandLab. “Optimized for desktop” and “Compatible with desktop” designations seem a little loose. Apple Music is optimized, but it doesn’t respond to right-clicks — only a click-and-hold brings up a context menu. And Firefox is compatible, which means it “works with standard mouse and keyboard controls,” yet it doesn’t respond to keyboard shortcuts for creating, deleting, or switching tabs. As expected, Googlebooks are best used with Google’s Chrome. [Image: It took a bunch of tries to get this prompt for installing the Slack progressive web app. And on one Googlebook it saved with the Slack logo, while on this one it saved with just a generic S icon. An app like Slack, which is acknowledged as “Better on the website,” is best used as a progressive web app install — just as it was on ChromeOS. But the web app couldn’t be installed at first while following the usual procedure I know from Chromebooks. After several attempts and starting from scratch by loading up slack.com, Chrome eventually prompted me to install it. This still feels like a speedy Chromebook with nifty new phone integrations [Image: “Hey, remember me? Can I be a Googlebook too?” If I never heard of Googlebooks and you dropped me in front of one of these laptops I’d figure ChromeOS just got a nice upgrade. They feel very Chromebook-ish. That’s not really a bad thing, as I’ve enjoyed Chromebooks for their relatively fuss-free web use. But that also means Googlebooks come with some old trappings of ChromeOS. Just like on Chromebooks, Chrome on Googlebooks doesn’t support separate Google accounts. You can have multiple Google accounts signed into the Googlebook, but there’s no wall between their browsing, bookmarks, and settings on Chrome like on Windows and macOS. The quirks that really irk [Image: [Image: App folders and right-click menus opened on the desktop don’t overlay above your windows, so they’re often partially hidden, and they stay open until you click on the desktop. They act this way on all the Googlebooks we’ve tested, whether using the mouse or using touch. What are we even doing here, Google? And this might mostly be a “me” problem, but I can’t remap the Caps Lock key to Ctrl on a Googlebook, even though that worked just fine on ChromeOS. In fact, none of the remappings for Ctrl, Caps Lock, Alt, or Action (the Google ‘G’ key) seem to work. They’re only remapped on external keyboards — despite the fact that the OS setting for “Modifier keys” is listed under “Physical keyboards.” I confirmed this by plugging in a mechanical keyboard. Android doesn’t seem to account for the keyboards built into these Googlebooks. And frankly, it’s driving me bonkers. (Look, I’ve got very specific muscle memory to maintain.) [Image: These settings do nothing for the built-in physical keyboard. And to be sure, I tested it on three different Googlebooks. I actually stayed up late trying to work my way around this by having Antigravity vibe code an Android app for me to remap Caps Lock to Ctrl, and after several failed attempts and a software-bricked HP keyboard I gave up. (It’s fine, it’s fine. The HP Googlebook’s keyboard works again after I uninstalled the useless app and restarted the laptop.) Quirks aside, Googlebooks are filled with cool ideas about how get-shit-done computers can interact with the everyday computers that live in our pockets and purses. An ongoing theme playing in my head when using these laptops is: “When this thing works, it works well. When this thing works well, it’s friggin’ sick.” But this OS still feels in a bit of a half-baked state. It needs much more polishing and development, and, ideally, lots of buy-in from developers. Google finds itself in yet another vicious software cycle: it needs developers to help solidify a better user experience, but will developers do that when there might not be tons of users lining up to be Google’s early adopters and glorified beta testers?

articles.title: Alexa can’t control the aux input on Amazon Echo speakers anymore
articles.summary: Amazon is disabling Alexa voice commands for control of the 3.5mm aux input on Echo speakers.
articles.body: If you’ve been using an older Amazon Echo device as a speaker through its 3.5mm aux input, Alexa voice commands to play or pause from line in may stop working. Ars Technica points to this Reddit poster claiming they received a message from Amazon about the change, which the company has confirmed. According to Amazon spokesperson Claudia Chavira Velez, “We recently notified the very small number of customers using voice requests to play or pause audio from the aux audio input on select Echo devices that this functionality will no longer be supported.” [Media: The message does not include any explanation for why the feature was removed. It also doesn’t mention any changes to audio output functionality like connecting an external speaker to an Echo Dot. Amazon’s statement notes that the physical connection still works on the devices that have the port: Echo Plus (2nd gen), Echo (3rd gen), Echo (4th gen), and Echo Studio (1st gen). Owners can control it from within the Alexa app, as well as pair Bluetooth speakers. As Ars Technica points out, it’s been years since Amazon released an Echo speaker with a 3.5mm aux port, and last year, Amazon also removed an Echo feature that allowed users to opt out of sending voice recordings to the cloud. Update, October 6th: Added comment from Amazon.

articles.title: Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y can be a backup battery for your house
articles.summary: Tesla has enabled Powershare vehicle-to-load charging for some Model 3 and Model Y vehicles if your home also has its Powerwall 3 battery.
articles.body: Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla’s expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla’s Powerwall 3. However, support for the Powerwall 2 and Powerwall Plus is “coming soon.” Tesla’s EVs aren’t the first or only ones with bidirectional charging; companies like Kia and GM also offer vehicle-to-home power on their vehicles, while Nissan’s Leaf offered power-to-grid charging years ago. Tesla says the Model 3 and Model Y can extend home backup power to over two days for Premium and Performance models, which is shorter than the “over three days” Tesla claims you can get from the Cybertruck’s battery. [Media: As Electrek points out, Tesla is only guaranteeing Home Backup will work on Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered from October 1st onward because not all older models include the PCS2 Lite inverter required to make it all work. So far, the feature is also only mentioned as available in the US and Puerto Rico, but not Canada, and not for the larger Model S or Model X. Tesla’s Powershare Grid Support feature is also still exclusive to the Cybertruck.

articles.title: Kaun Banega Crorepati 18: Madhuri Dixit revisits Amitabh Bachchan’s ‘Ek Do Teen’ dance from Toofan; Big B jokes, ‘Kahan-kahan se yeh log nikal ke la rahe hain’
articles.summary: Amitabh Bachchan was in for an unexpected throwback on Kaun Banega Crorepati 18 when Madhuri Dixit revisited one of his most unusual dance performances.
articles.body: Amitabh Bachchan was in for an unexpected throwback on Kaun Banega Crorepati 18 when Madhuri Dixit revisited one of his most unusual dance performances. The actress had the megastar watch an old clip of himself attempting the iconic ‘Ek Do Teen’ steps, leaving him laughing and visibly embarrassed.During their conversation on the show, Amitabh recalled an instance when he had tried to recreate the popular dance move. Looking back at the memory, he said, “Ek baar humse badi gustakhi ho gayi thi. Ek film thi, humne woh… 1, 2, 3 aise peeche hat ke kiya tha.”Madhuri, intrigued by Amitabh’s recollection, asked to see the footage. The show’s team soon played the old clip, catching the veteran actor off guard.The footage was from Amitabh’s 1989 film Toofan, in which he performed a comic rendition of the dance associated with Madhuri’s ‘Ek Do Teen’. In the scene, the actor appears in a woman’s avatar and attempts the signature hip movements and steps from the popular number.As the clip played, Amitabh could not contain his laughter. Reacting to his younger self, the actor jokingly criticised his own attempt and said, “Arey baap re… Kahan-kahan se yeh log nikal ke la rahe hain… Ek acche gaane ko kis tarah kharab kiya jaaye, woh idhar dekha aapne abhi.”The original ‘Ek Do Teen’ featured Madhuri as Mohini in N Chandra’s 1988 film Tezaab. Sung by Alka Yagnik and Amit Kumar, the song was composed by Laxmikant-Pyarelal, with Saroj Khan choreographing Madhuri’s now-iconic performance.Madhuri appeared on Kaun Banega Crorepati 18 as part of Amitabh’s birthday celebrations on the show. articles.title: Jaguar’s Type 01 EV looks just like its divisive concept car
articles.summary: The Type 01 goes on sale next year for $130,000.
articles.body: The Type 01, Jaguar’s most important and divisive car in years, has arrived. The production follow-up to the polarising Type 00 concept, Jaguar says the electric, four-door grand tourer is its most powerful road car ever. Even though the Type 00’s design chief was reportedly fired earlier this year, most of its aesthetic has carried over to the final car, for better or worse. You can’t buy it in that hot Miami pink though — didn’t anyone tell them GTA VI is almost here? It has the same low-slung silhouette, extended side-profile, and huge 23-inch wheels as the prototype, though shifting to a four-door design makes those proportions feel more natural. On the inside, leather and brass detailing run throughout. A 24-inch OLED display sits behind the steering wheel, with additional 7-inch, smartphone-style screens in the central spine, one in the front and one in the back, with controls for climate, audio, and seats. With no true rear window, there’s another display instead, rising out of the “panoramic soundbar” to display the feed from a rear-facing camera. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Under the hood, three electric motors (one front, two rear) combine to deliver up to 1,016 horsepower and 1,365Nm of torque, going from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds, and from there to 112mph in a further 4.0 seconds. The 118kWh battery should deliver a range of up to 400 miles, and 350kW DC charging should get back 200 miles of range in as little as 13 minutes. Orders for the Type 01 are expected to open in early 2027, with cars shipping in the second half of the year. Full pricing hasn’t been announced, but Jaguar has opened signups to register interest, teasing that one variant will cost $130,500. [Media: Correction, October 7th: An earlier version of this article misstated that the Type 01 is Jaguar’s first EV. It released the electric I-Pace in 2018.

articles.title: At $1,279, Google’s Xreal Aura will go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses
articles.summary: Xreal has just opened Aura pre-orders starting at $1,279, making its Android XR device just $20 less than the Meta VR Glasses.
articles.body: Two weeks ago, journalists in the San Francisco Bay Area got to try two hot new wearables that weigh only around 100 grams: the just-revealed Meta VR Glasses, and the long-awaited transparent Google XR glasses built in partnership with Xreal. It turns out they’re going head-to-head. Xreal has just opened Aura pre-orders starting at $1,279, $20 less than the Meta VR Glasses. That’s for the Xreal Aura with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage; there’ll also be a 16GB / 512GB config for $1,499. (Xreal couldn’t tell us whether the 16GB of RAM would be important for some apps by publish time.) Both the Google / Xreal Aura and Meta’s VR Glasses let you overlay virtual objects and desktops on the real world. Both are relatively lightweight because they’ve got a cord — their Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chips and batteries both live in a compute puck, which runs either Meta’s Horizon OS or Android XR. Both greet you with a grid of floating app icons to choose from. [Image: But they’re very different experiences in practice, primarily because the Google / Xreal Aura has transparent lenses, while the Meta VR Glasses use passthrough vision to let you see the real world and offers more immersion. While the Xreal Aura has one of the largest transparent fields of view yet at 70 degrees diagonal, it’s still smaller than Meta’s passthrough glasses. I wrote all about it in this story, and it’s just one of many differences. The Meta VR Glasses also have eye tracking, like the Apple Vision Pro, so you can select things just by looking at them and pinching fingers resting on your lap; the Google / Xreal Aura has a touchpad built into the compute puck and hand-tracking to give you virtual laser pointers. (Both let you connect to other peripherals and display other devices too — and you can plug devices with USB-C DisplayPort video right in.) And, of course, you’ve got your Android apps inside the Xreal Aura, or your Quest games inside the VR Glasses. I don’t think any journalist can tell you which is better yet; you may want to wait for reviews. We also have yet to test Android XR extensively: while Samsung and Google did technically ship the $1,799 Galaxy XR with Android XR last year, they didn’t send one to The Verge for review. The Meta VR Glasses aren’t due until spring 2027, but Xreal isn’t necessarily shipping lots of pairs before then. Today, the only people who can preorder the Xreal glasses are those who already put in a reservation, and only the first 2,000 “Founder’s Edition” pairs are necessarily coming at “launch.” Those will ship this year, Xreal CEO and co-founder Chi Xu tells The Verge. [Image: It might not take till the end of the year. Xreal’s press release does say they “will begin shipping soon” and that the “launch” is “now just weeks away,” but those are wiggly, and again, those timeframes are just for early adopters. If you don’t have a preorder, “Orders will open to the general public in the coming weeks.” The glasses will also only ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea to start, before expanding to other regions in 2027. I’m already a fan of Xreal’s older glasses and how they let me watch my 3D movies with a 57-degree field of view, and I’m intrigued by the puck. I’d love to see how much more useful these glasses are with the new 70-degree view.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel Buds update will put them to sleep along with you
articles.summary: Plus new voice controls, and one-tap microphone muting and live translation, for the Buds 2A and Pro 2.
articles.body: Google has detailed an update bringing a slew of new features to its Pixel Buds 2A and Pro 2, which the company says are rolling out now. The new features were first teased in August. The biggest update is Pixel Watch-powered sleep detection, rolling out to both pairs of earbuds. If you’re wearing a Pixel Watch, the buds will now react when you fall asleep, by pausing music, silencing notifications, and turning off touch controls. Several other updates are also coming to both the Buds 2A and Pro. Tap-to-mute allows you to mute or unmute your microphone with a quick tap during calls, though only when also using a Pixel phone, and you can now activate live translation with a single tap. New Gemini voice commands will allow you to control active noise cancellation (ANC), adjust the EQ, or turn on touch controls. The final new feature is Dynamic ANC, which will adjust audio and ANC levels based on the quality of the buds’ seal in your ears. This is exclusive to the Buds Pro 2. Google announced the update rollout in a Pixel Buds community forum post. The original version of the announcement, posted yesterday, said that all the features except Dynamic ANC would also be coming to the original Pixel Buds Pro, but all mention of those earbuds has now been removed from the post. articles.title: Amazon uses its tracking data to guess whether shoppers have a flat butt and no friends
articles.summary: Amazon’s “About You” section is going viral after one user found that the ecommerce giant thinks she has “flat buttocks” based on her shopping history.
articles.body: Most people know that Amazon collects data about your shopping history to serve up personalized product recommendations. But what some of us didn’t realize is that you can check exactly what Amazon knows — or thinks it knows — about you in your settings menu. One user’s findings went viral on Threads after she discovered that Amazon assumed she “has flat buttocks” based on her purchases, resulting in a flood of other posts with users sharing the oddly specific information Amazon uses to describe them. In another post, a user found that Amazon says they don’t “trust people easily,” while someone else discovered that Amazon thinks she “finds it hilarious when toys get stuck to ceiling tiles in the classroom.” Other descriptions spotted by users include “cusses when scared,” “cannot keep real plants alive,” “has no friends,” and “treats cats as biological children.” [Media: While some of these descriptions seem like a roast from Amazon, most of them are pretty generic. For example, mine says I “maintain active aquarium systems,” “regularly consume coffee,” and “play video games regularly,” all of which are accurate. If you want to see what Amazon may have learned about you, you can find out by selecting your account icon in the top-right corner of your screen, scrolling down to the “Your Account” section, and hitting “Your Shopping preferences.” From there, scroll down the page and select “About You.” You’ll then see a list of details Amazon uses to personalize your account, which you can edit or delete.

articles.title: Ring’s first smart lock can be charged by turning a dial when the battery unexpectedly dies
articles.summary: Amazon’s new Ring Smart Lock offers several ways to unlock your door but eliminates the need for keys with a built-in hand-cranked battery charger.
articles.body: Amazon announced its first smart lock that eliminates the need for a physical backup key should its rechargeable battery die while you’re away from home. While other smart locks lean on hidden USB ports or metal contacts for connecting a 9-volt battery to replenish a dead battery, the new Ring Smart Lock incorporates a more convenient charger right into its thumb-turn dial. Amazon doesn’t specify how many turns are needed but claims just “a few times” can generate enough power to unlock the door so you can gain access to your home and fully recharge the lock’s battery. The Ring Smart Lock is expected to be available in the US sometime in early 2027 (pending FCC approval) and will be offered in black, silver, and brass finishes for $249. Unlocking options include a fingerprint reader and a backlit touchscreen keypad with the option to register multiple users and schedule when they have access to your home. This includes setting up temporary access codes that automatically expire after a set amount of time. The Ring Smart Lock can also be opened, locked, and monitored using the Ring mobile app or controlled using voice commands through Alexa-compatible devices like Echo smart speakers. Installation doesn’t require any wiring since the Smart Lock uses Ring’s replaceable Quick Release Ultra Battery Pack, and instead of relying on your home’s Wi-Fi, the lock wirelessly connects to other devices using Amazon’s low-power, low-bandwidth, long-range Sidewalk network. Assuming you live somewhere with adequate Sidewalk coverage, you won’t have to worry about Wi-Fi outages preventing you from granting remote access or getting alerts about who’s just entered your home. [Image: From left: The $150 Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, the $200 Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, the $220 Floodlight Cam 4K Plus, and the $100 Indoor Cam 4K. The Ring Smart Lock doesn’t include a camera, so you’ll need to pair it with a smart doorbell to see who’s accessing your home or one of five new Ring security cameras expanding Amazon’s collection of “Retinal Vision 4K” devices that first debuted a year ago. Starting today, you can preorder the new $149.99 Outdoor Cam 4K Plus that’s available in battery, wired, solar, and PoE versions, the $199.99 Spotlight Cam 4K Plus featuring a 550-lumen deterrent light, and the $219.99 Floodlight Cam 4K Plus that can illuminate large spaces while offering 24/7 recording with smart subject detection. But you won’t have to wait for the first indoor Ring camera with Retinal 4K. The $99.99 Indoor Cam 4K is available for purchase today and features a 115-degree field of view with a shutter that physically blocks the camera when privacy is needed. [Image: The Ring Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K can be mounted to a wall or used self-standing, but tethered access to a power source is required. Alongside all the new 4K options, Amazon is also introducing a new entry-level 2K indoor camera that’s available starting today for $69.99. The Ring Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K uses “computer vision–based motion detection” to track subjects like pets moving around a room. The camera can rotate a full 360 degrees while tilting 175 degrees to keep subjects in frame, and like Ring’s new 4K indoor camera, the 2K version incorporates a physical privacy shutter that disables both the camera and its microphone when it’s closed.

articles.title: Ring's first smart lock can be hand-cranked when its battery dies | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amazon-owned Ring is entering the smart lock market with a device designed to tackle a common concern: getting locked out when the battery dies.
articles.body:
Ring, the Amazon-owned video doorbell maker, is entering a new market: smart locks.

Ring’s new device isn’t exactly a copy-and-paste of the other locks already on the market, however, as it tackles a big issue that often deters people from embracing this kind of smart home equipment: the fear of the battery dying and getting locked out.

To address this, Ring’s smart lock has added a power dial. If the battery on the device runs out, the homeowner can just turn the dial a few times to power the lock back up and enter their home.

Ring’s founder Jamie Siminoff said the idea to rethink smart locks came to him when he was looking to buy a lock for a vacation home. “I struggled because this particular house will get used very little, and I know the freaking battery will die on it,” he said.

He also worried that family or friends visiting the house might get stuck outside, as the door isn’t connected to a power source, and any smart lock would be dependent on the battery.

“I’m like, well, why don’t we just fix this,” he said. Using AI, he started working on a project to create a lock you could hand-crank just enough to power the lock to open. Once you’re in, you could then take out the rechargeable battery pack and charge it as usual.

Siminoff says the battery on Ring’s new lock will last about a year, and will alert users when it’s time to charge via the Ring app. The app also allows users to configure access for people who may need periodic access, like dog walkers or house cleaners. Eventually, the company wants to allow third-party app makers to design specialized software for the lock so it can be used in other ways — for example, Airbnb owners who may need to regularly change codes.

The Ring lock also offers four different ways to get in, so you won’t have to worry about forgetting a code. You can either use the device’s fingerprint reader, a backlit touchscreen keypad, the Ring app, or Alexa.

Siminoff admitted that the lock may be comparable to others on the market, but he thinks the fact that it addresses the anxiety over being locked out will be its biggest selling point.

“I do think the power thing is a huge limiter of why people are not buying, and why they’re not putting them in, and why they’re worried about them,” he said.

It’s also true that when smart locks do offer some sort of backup method, they usually involve something cumbersome and less secure — like hiding a physical key somewhere on the property.

Ring’s smart lock will fit a standard single-cylinder deadbolt and will be available to purchase in the U.S. in the first quarter of 2027, after it receives FCC authorization. It will come in three finishes: black, silver, or brass.

Alongside the lock, Ring also introduced four new 4K cameras: the Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus, and a pan-tilt Indoor Cam 4K.

articles.title: Tony Fadell on why the first wave of AI gadgets failed — and what comes next | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The “father of the iPod” says the first generation of AI gadgets failed to solve real problems — and the next wave will need to earn consumers’ trust.
articles.body:
When Tony Fadell takes the stage at the inaugural MIT Future Fest , he projects a slide with three images of once-hyped AI devices that have already been discontinued: the Rabbit R1, the Humane Ai pin, and the Limitless pendant.

“These were kind of the ‘Gen 1’ AI products, and because of my background, these companies called me and asked me to help them,” Fadell said. “I didn’t.”

It’s no surprise that these companies want Fadell’s advice. He’s credited as the “father of the iPod,” a co-creator of the iPhone, and the founder of Nest, the smart thermostat company acquired by Google.

“You have to really understand what you’re trying to do, what pain you’re trying to solve,” he said. “In each of these cases, each one of them didn’t meet any kind of need — it was just interesting technology for geeks, and you’re like, ‘Okay, that’s neat, but it doesn’t really apply to my life.’”

These early AI devices promised the convenience of having a personal assistant, but didn’t actually work that well. Even if they did, most people have never had an assistant and know how they would use — or grow to trust — a personal robot helper.

“It’s less than 0.01% of the world population that has ever had a human [assistant] do anything, and so when [companies] say, ‘Oh, we want an assistant,’ that’s a bunch of people who have assistants saying it,” he said. “Most consumers don’t even know what an assistant is.”

Fadell goes on to explain to those of us in the 99.99% that hiring a trustworthy personal assistant isn’t as straightforward as pulling the most promising resume out of a pile of applications.

“It took me a couple of years first to understand how best to utilize [an assistant], and then to trust them with the most sensitive data, and have them be an agent where they’re setting up meetings with people and working with my bank,” he said. “I understand we have this vision of the future, but there’s a lot of steps to get the general consumer and even the general business on this path.”

It’s hard to talk about the struggles of building trust in your personal assistant without sounding a bit entitled, but Fadell has a point. When you hire a human assistant, you’re not giving them your bank account login on day one. We’re heading into a world where anyone can have a personal AI assistant, but these tools are only valuable if we can trust them to be completely secure.

At this point, establishing trust with an AI assistant seems even harder than relying on a human. Meta recently launched Muse , its all-purpose AI assistant, but users have reason to be wary. A security researcher quickly found a serious vulnerability in Muse after launch, and a recent 404 Media report states that some Meta employees discovered security issues that prompted multiple teams to embark upon a “mad dash” to fix these problems before launch, working overtime.

“Trust and safety are going to be paramount with anything that we turn over to some kind of intelligence,” Fadell said. “The only company I could see right now — maybe one other — is Apple who could do this. Apple has all the hardware, they have all the chips, they have all the pieces, but they don’t have all the AI stuff.”

Even if it’s not Apple that ultimately produces the stickiest AI agent, Fadell predicts that a successful agent will have to operate on-device only, both for the sake of privacy and to keep the tech lightweight.

“When you’re hearing all of these things about, ‘Oh, data centers are going to conquer the world,’ … I don’t believe it,” he said. “I’ve seen this before. I’ve seen this play out in the internet days and what have you. We have so much power on the device now, and even more compute, and they’re still battery operated.”

By keeping sensitive data on-device, rather than transmitting it through the cloud, Apple has garnered trust from users to share their biometric data through features like Face ID. As Fadell notes, Apple seems to have more goodwill with consumers than its competitors when it comes to privacy, but unlike other top tech companies, Apple doesn’t have a world-class AI model of its own — the new Siri AI runs on custom-built versions of Google’s Gemini.

While Apple lags in proprietary AI, it is leaps ahead in hardware. Fadell theorizes that companies like Meta and OpenAI are turning their attention toward gadgets because they don’t have billions of devices in circulation like Apple does.

“It’s because they don’t have access to the sensors on your phone. They’re like, ‘Oh, we’ll need video,’ and you have to check, ‘Yes, I’ll give you video.’ Then they say, ‘Well, we need audio.’ Check. ‘We need your GPS location.’ Check. And before you know it, it becomes a list of 20 things or more than you have then allowed them to have,” he said. “So what do they do? They go and make a device with all that stuff in it without a screen… and then they just Bluetooth or Wi-Fi into your phone and then back up to the web, or into a 5G network, so they can get all the sensor data.”

Given his history creating the iPhone and iPod, it might seem like Fadell is still looking at his former employer through rose-colored glasses. While he may give Apple credit where due, he hasn’t been shy to call Apple out when he thinks they’re messing up.

When an audience member asks about the luck involved in finding product-market fit, Fadell points out that it’s more difficult for startups to manufacture that luck, since a failed product can spell the end of the company.

“Because it’s a startup, you get one shot,” he quipped. “It’s not like Apple with the Vision Pro.”

After scrapping its proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging on its smaller Surface devices last year, the Surface Laptop Ultra has a charging cable that attaches magnetically to the right side USB-C port. During Microsoft’s Windows event on Wednesday, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri said that you can just “bring the connector close, and it snaps right into place.“ It’s still a proprietary solution, but the USB-C port it slots into still works for video, data, and other USB-C connectivity like you’d expect. Microsoft is calling it Magnetic Connect, and I’m surprised the company hasn’t shortened that to Mag-C. Microsoft first announced its Surface Laptop Ultra earlier this year. It comes equipped with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip, which is capable of handling gaming, creative workloads, and on-device AI models. articles.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000
articles.summary: Prices start much lower, but 128GB of unified memory is going to really cost you.
articles.body: The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match. The flagship Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark laptops from Dell, Lenovo, MSI, HP, and Asus start as low as $2,599 for configurations with an 18-core CPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage. That’s close in price to a similarly specced 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, though Apple includes 1TB of storage. But the prices for both RTX Spark and Apple laptops of course go much, much higher. Of the pricing we’ve seen so far, a kitted-out Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark laptop with a 20-core chip, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage costs up to $6,999.99. We don’t yet know the full breadth of configuration options for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, as the preorder page only has an email sign-up box to get updates, but a 48GB model on Best Buy costs $3,999.99. [Image: Asus’ ProArt P14 and P16 range in price from $2,599.99 to $6,999.99. Wildly expensive laptops aren’t really anything new: you can configure a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max chip to nearly $10,000 if you max out all options. But the first volley of RTX Spark options are obviously aimed at the high-end side of creators and local AI users. And RAMageddon certainly isn’t helping make this any easier on peoples’ wallets. Will they be worth it? We’ll find out soon. The Surface Laptop Ultra and other RTX Spark laptops are launching this month — as early as October 16th.

articles.title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11 | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its Surface Laptop Ultra, AI PCs that run on Nvidia chips that are designed to run AI models and agents.
articles.body:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)

Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.

The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.

Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”

He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”

The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.

Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.

Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

articles.title: BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
articles.summary: BMW announced the iX4, a sportier spin on the iX3 and the latest Neue Klasse vehicle with a next-gen battery. BMW says the new EV can get up to 428 miles of range.
articles.body: While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV that puts a sportier spin on the automaker’s iX3. The iX4 is the third vehicle to be released on BMW’s next-generation Neue Klasse platform, following the iX3 and i3 models. The iX4 50 xDrive will come first in March 2027, followed by an even more high-performance M60 xDrive version later in the year. The automaker is positioning this new lineup as its bulwark against the flood of Chinese imports that is currently decimating other European brands. But while the iX4 can certainly compete on range and tech, it’s unclear whether BMW can rival China in terms of sheer affordability. In that respect, the BMW iX4 50 xDrive starts at $66,200 (excluding fees for destination and handling). And it bears all the hallmarks of BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, such as the “Gen6” high-voltage battery with 112.2kWh of usable energy, an 800-volt architecture for lightning-quick charging top-ups, and up to 428 miles of range based on EPA estimates. That’s more range than the Tesla Model Y, the best-selling electric vehicle in the world. BMW has been blowing away expectations on range to such a degree that even the experts at InsideEVs are left wondering whether it’s overkill. After all, Tesla and others have done plenty well with EVs in the mid-300s, while Lucid continues to struggle despite exceeding 500 miles in range. [Image: The BMW iX4 50 xDrive (left) and M60 xDrive (right). But BMW wants to go the distance, believing that range and efficiency are two of its biggest selling points. The third would be performance, and thanks to a dual-motor setup in both the 50 xDrive and M60 xDrive, the iX4 is sure to delivery plenty of giddy up. The 50 xDrive’s motors put out 463 horsepower and 475lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60mph acceleration of 4.7 seconds. Meanwhile, the M60 xDrive’s motors produce 603hp and 645lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60 time a whole second less than the 50 xDrive. Like other Neue Klasse vehicles, the electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) in the rear axle serves as the primary drive axle, using electricity instead of permanent magnets to power both its stator outer frame and interior spinning rotor. An inverter acts as the brain of the system, converting direct current from the battery into alternating current for the motor, regulating the electromagnets, and monitoring performance to keep the motor running as efficiently as possible. BMW says this combination helps slash drive-system energy losses by 40 percent and weight by 10 percent. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Gen6 batteries are built with cylindrical lithium-ion cells measuring 46mm in diameter and 95mm in height that provide a 20 percent increase in energy density compared to the prismatic cells used in BMW’s Gen5 batteries. BMW has eliminated the traditional modules in favor of a “pack-to-open-body” construction where the battery housing serves as the vehicle’s underbody, lowering weight and increasing torsional rigidity. Like Hyundai and Kia, BMW is building its Neue Klasse EVs to take fast charging to the next level. With its 800V architecture, the iX4 can accept up to 400kWs of DC fast charging, replenishing up to 184 miles of range in 10 minutes, and 10–80 percent charge in just 21 minutes. With a NACS charging port, the iX4 will be compatible with over 80,000 Tesla Supercharger connectors around the world. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Panoramic iDrive infotainment system is BMW’s redesigned digital dashboard that replaces traditional gauge clusters with a heads-up-style projection along the full width of the lower windshield. The 17.9-inch central touchscreen presents as a free-cut display where you can drag and drop up to six widgets like media, weather, or navigation from the screen directly onto the windshield display. And like the i3 and iX3, the iX4 can do all sorts of extra stuff, including bidirectional charging with vehicle-to-load and vehicle-to-home capabilities, an intelligent charging flap that opens when a driver approaches a known charging point, and Plug & Charge for automatic charging at 10 different charging providers. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: If you look at the whole package, there’s a lot to like. Sure, the Model Y beats the iX4 in a few categories, most importantly price. It’s a bit quicker off the line, and of course, the Model Y comes with the option for Full Self-Driving (Supervised). BMW has something it calls “Symbiotic Drive,” which it describes as a Level 2 system designed for “fluid, intuitive interaction.” In other words, drivers can adjust the steering or even brake without canceling the automated functions. The iX4 also allows for hands-free driving on the highway — but no point-to-point assisted driving. Not until 2027 at the earliest. Where BMW still bests Tesla is variety. You can get the iX4 50 xDrive, or if you want something sportier, try the M60 xDrive. If you’re rather have a sedan, there’s the i3. Or if you want something a bit more affordable, there’s the iX3. And don’t forget the flagship 7 series. Yep, those are getting Neue Klasse makeovers as well. Tesla has the Model 3 and Model Y — and that’s about it. (Yes, there’s the Cybertruck, but clearly most people aren’t interested in that. And there’s the Cybercab, but it won’t be on sale anytime soon.) BMW knows its customers want options. And it’s doing it’s best to deliver.
